title: Expressing Confidence in a Team Members Abilities After a Poor Performance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that compassionate leaders go beyond the standard post-mistake conversation of listening and offering a new game plan. The author's central claim is that the most powerful move a leader can make after a colleague's poor performance is to state, specifically and unequivocally, that they still believe in that person's talent. Generic reassurance does little; specificity is what lands. The piece contrasts this direct verbal affirmation with the more common but slower-acting practice of demonstrating belief through future assignments, arguing that words spoken immediately have an impact that assignments given later cannot match. It closes by framing belief as something that only counts if it is actually voiced aloud.
points: Belief in a team member only has impact if it is spoken aloud immediately after a setback, not implied through future assignments.
Specificity is the mechanism: naming exact past successes and named skills makes the affirmation credible rather than empty encouragement.
Assigning someone to a future project functions as a slower, delayed form of endorsement compared to a direct verbal statement.
quotes: Perhaps nothing boosts the morale and self-confidence of a team member more than when they hear from their leader that they believe in their talents, especially after a poor performance.
They remind them of their past successes and milestones, describing the accomplishments they were particularly impressed by.
Believing in a colleague doesn’t mean as much if they never hear about it.
A leader who talks about their belief has an immediate impact and boosts confidence so that it lasts.
In the workplace, nothing matches a leader’s belief in the skills and talents of a colleague after a weak performance.
